title: TrainMind — User Guide
subtitle: Basketball strength and conditioning: from planning to return to play

scenes.caption: TrainMind — User Guide
scenes.text: TrainMind is the platform a strength and conditioning coach uses to plan, record and read a basketball team's work. In this video we'll go through the coach app and, at the end, the athlete app. Everything you'll see is computed from a single measure: internal load, that is session RPE multiplied by actual duration.

scenes.caption: Creating the account
scenes.text: It starts with registration. Besides your personal details you need the organization name: it is the club's workspace, where teams, athletes and plans will live. Whoever registers becomes its administrator. The two mandatory consents are terms and privacy; the third one, on health and fitness data, is what switches on the artificial intelligence features, performance analysis and wellness.

scenes.caption: Logging in
scenes.text: Signing in is email and password. The selector at the top right switches the language between Italian, English and Spanish, and it works before login too.

scenes.caption: Three areas: menu, team selector, top bar
scenes.text: The interface has three fixed areas. The menu on the left. Under the logo, the team selector, which filters the whole application: pick a team and dashboard, wellness, analytics and reports narrow to it. At the top, global search and the profile menu.

scenes.caption: The Dashboard
scenes.text: The dashboard is the snapshot of the moment. The tiles count athletes, sessions, injuries and active protocols. But the part that matters is the at-risk athletes panel: the criterion is the ratio between acute and chronic load, what everyone calls A C W R, and wellness is there to confirm, not to pass sentence.

scenes.caption: Why wellness alone is not enough
scenes.text: Alessandro Baldini is in red, above one point five: he has worked far more than his own average of the last three weeks. The label says why — load spike. A two out of five in wellness after a bad night tells you nothing about injury risk; the ratio between how much he has worked and how much he is used to working does.

scenes.caption: Teams and rosters
scenes.text: Teams take seconds to create and each has its own roster. An athlete training with two teams should be added from existing, not duplicated: otherwise tests, wellness and load history split in two.

scenes.caption: The athlete record
scenes.text: The athlete record gathers personal details, measurements, physical performance and injuries. The invitation to the athlete app starts from here too.

scenes.caption: Tests and measurements
scenes.text: Every test shows the latest value, the change against the previous measurement and the history of testing dates. The practical advice is to test the whole team on the same day with the same protocol: aligned dates are what make charts comparable.

scenes.caption: The calendar
scenes.text: The calendar is the team diary: training, games, shooting sessions, rehab, medical appointments. At the top you see the active periodization, with the current mesocycle and the deload weeks. An event moves by dragging it onto another day.

scenes.caption: Periodization
scenes.text: Periodization is the macro-structure of the season: pre-season, league, playoffs, off-season, each with its mesocycles and the load percentage that governs progression.

scenes.caption: Inside a mesocycle
scenes.text: Inside a mesocycle there are the weeks and, in each of them, the sessions with duration, exercise count and RPE. The bar at the top tells you where the plan stands.

scenes.caption: Generating a plan with AI
scenes.text: A mesocycle can also be generated by artificial intelligence, giving it the season phase, the goal, the duration and the training days. The result is an editable draft: read it and correct it, do not apply it blind.

scenes.caption: The exercise library
scenes.text: Exercises live in a single library, split by category: cardio, strength, plyometrics, technique. Each one carries its muscle groups and equipment, and on the top plan you can ask the assistant to suggest new ones. These are the exercises you then pull into sessions.

scenes.caption: Inside a session
scenes.text: Open a session and you see the exercises in order, each with sets, reps, load and rest. On bodyweight movements the load field becomes the added load: leave it empty and it means bodyweight only. At the top sit the duration, the RPE and the intensity note from the plan.

scenes.caption: Training on court
scenes.text: This is the page to keep open on a tablet courtside. Every player has a traffic light — available, reduced load, out — and their own RPE. At the top you see how many are available out of the whole roster.

scenes.caption: A timer per exercise
scenes.text: Each exercise has its own timer: start, stop, work time and rest. At the end the totals are the real ones, not the planned ones, and each athlete's load is written when you complete the session.

scenes.caption: Game minutes
scenes.text: For games there is the minutes sheet, with quarters, any overtime and the clock: from there come minutes, RPE and load for every player.

scenes.caption: Wellness
scenes.text: Wellness is filled in by the athlete every morning: sleep, fatigue, soreness, stress, mood. The scale is uniform across all items — five is always the best condition — so nobody has to remember that on one item high is good and on another it is bad.

scenes.caption: Registering an injury
scenes.text: When something happens, the injury is registered with type, area, severity and clinical notes. The app proposes a return protocol on its own, based on area, type and severity, with the phases involved and the estimated date.

scenes.caption: Return-to-Play
scenes.text: The Return-to-Play protocol is made of phases and clearance criteria. You advance only when the mandatory criteria are met, and every step stays on record with who decided it and when. This is the part you need when you have to explain to someone else why a player went back on court that day.

scenes.caption: The protocol library
scenes.text: Return-to-play protocols are not written from scratch every time. The system library holds about twenty of them, by body area, injury type and severity. Duplicate one and the copy is yours, editable in every phase and every criterion: that is how you adapt a protocol to your own squad without losing the original.

scenes.caption: Analytics
scenes.text: The Analytics team tab distributes the roster across the load zones: optimal, caution, risk. It is the same reading as the dashboard, with filters for team, athlete and date range on top.

scenes.caption: ACWR over time
scenes.text: The A C W R chart shows the ratio over time, with the bands: below zero point eight is undertraining, between zero point eight and one point three is the optimal zone, above one point five is high risk.

scenes.caption: The wellness heatmap
scenes.text: The wellness heatmap puts one row per athlete and one column per day: this is the view that surfaces the hole, the row turning red for several days in a row.

scenes.caption: Attendance
scenes.text: The attendance tab says who was there and who was not, session by session, with the participation percentage, the average RPE and the accumulated load. It is what lets you read an athlete's numbers knowing how many sessions they rest on: an average over three training sessions is not worth what an average over fifteen is.

scenes.caption: The daily report
scenes.text: The daily report is the end-of-day sheet: activities carried out, each player's availability from zero to five, notes and guidelines for tomorrow. It exports to PDF or Word, and can be scheduled to go out by email automatically.

scenes.caption: Automatic reports
scenes.text: A report that has to be written by hand every day eventually stops being written. From the schedules you set the recipient, the frequency and the format, and the report goes out by email on its own: weekly to the coaching staff, monthly to the board, whatever you need.

scenes.caption: Alerts
scenes.text: Alert rules watch the data for you. You pick the metric — ACWR, wellness score, fatigue, soreness — the threshold and the direction of the comparison, and when the condition is met a notification arrives. It is how you avoid having to open the app every morning just to notice a problem.

scenes.caption: The AI assistant
scenes.text: The AI assistant knows your organization's exercise library and cites the sources it used. It is a consultant, not a decision-maker: you sign the programme.

scenes.caption: Proposed adaptations
scenes.text: Adaptations are the most concrete part of the AI: it looks at the previous sessions, the ACWR and the wellness, and proposes cutting volume or intensity on the next one. It always arrives as a proposal: you see it next to the original plan and decide whether to approve it, edit it or reject it. Nothing changes on its own.

scenes.caption: The athlete app
scenes.text: Now the athlete app. It installs on the phone straight from the browser, without going through the stores, and shows three things: whether today's wellness is filled in, what the next session is, and where the athlete stands in their own path.

scenes.caption: One minute in the morning
scenes.text: Daily wellness is five items and the hours of sleep: one minute in the morning, before training. It is the gesture that holds the whole monitoring system up.

scenes.caption: Assigned sessions
scenes.text: In sessions the athlete finds the exercises with sets, reps and loads, and can mark what was done and at what perceived effort.

scenes.caption: The athlete's history
scenes.text: In History the athlete looks back over thirty days of sessions and wellness entries. The percentage score is the same one you read in the heatmap: the five items added up, divided by twenty-five, times a hundred. Seeing their own consistency is the simplest way to show them that those five morning numbers do not disappear down a hole.

scenes.caption: The profile
scenes.text: In Profile the athlete finds their own card: position, number, height, weight, teams. These are read-only — you keep them up to date from the athlete record. The app language is changed from the menu at the top right, and it is independent of the one you use.

scenes.caption: Language and settings
scenes.text: One last thing: from Settings you change the theme and the interface language, between Italian, English and Spanish. The choice follows the account, not the device, so you find it the same from any computer.

scenes.caption: Good work
scenes.text: That is TrainMind: plan, record what actually happens on court, and read the numbers before they turn into an injury. The PDF guide that comes with this video goes into the detail of every screen. Good work.
